summary:
SPHEREx Blink is a public-facing web application that transforms NASA’s SPHEREx Level 2 near-infrared archive into an interactive time-domain discovery engine for citizen scientists and researchers. Since May 2025, SPHEREx has mapped the entire sky every six months across 102 spectral bands (0.75–5.0 µm) using six Linear Variable Filter (LVF) detector arrays (D1–D6), observing over a billion objects. However, raw exposures (~70 MB each) cannot be simply flipped as images due to spacecraft roll, optical distortion, zodiacal background, and the continuous LVF wavelength gradient across pixels.
Our tool solves this by querying NASA/IPAC IRSA cutouts, subtracting the zodiacal light model, filtering 32-bit artifact flags, and reprojecting visits onto a unified north-up tangent-plane (TAN) WCS grid. Users can blink multi-epoch co-adds at 60 FPS, compute real-time Float32 epoch differences and sums, overlay Gaia DR3 astrometry, and click any source to extract 102-channel spectra and light curves on the fly.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

SPHEREx Blink is an interactive web platform inspired by Backyard Worlds / WiseView and engineered specifically for the 3D chrono-spectral architecture of NASA's SPHEREx Level 2 Multi-Extension FITS (MEF) data. Users enter any sky coordinates (RA/Dec in decimal degrees or sexagesimal format) or object name to inspect how the infrared sky changes across six-month survey epochs.

Because SPHEREx uses Linear Variable Filters (LVFs) where wavelength varies continuously across detector pixels and visits occur at arbitrary spacecraft roll angles, raw exposures cannot be directly blinked without geometric and spectral alignment. Our five-stage server-to-browser pipeline addresses this:

1. Live IRSA TAP Discovery & Cutout Streaming: Queries NASA/IPAC IRSA (spherex.artifact joined with spherex.plane) across all six detector arrays (SPHEREx-D1 through SPHEREx-D6) and streams targeted FITS cutouts (?center=RA,Dec&size=FOV), reducing ~70 MB full-frame exposures to lightweight kilobyte cutouts.

2. Zodiacal Light Subtraction & Dynamic Bitmask Cleaning: Computes Clean = IMAGE - ZODI, removes residual sky pedestals, and parses 32-bit MSKN* bitmask definitions from FLAGS headers (TRANSIENT, OVERFLOW, NONLINEAR, GHOST, STREAK, SNOWBALL). Bad pixels are repaired via 3x3 median filtering prior to interpolation while preserving saturated stellar cores.

3. North-Up Tangent-Plane (TAN) Reprojection & Adaptive Epoch Clustering: Reprojects all exposures onto a unified North-Up, East-Left gnomonic grid (RA---TAN, DEC--TAN) at SPHEREx's native 6.2"/pixel scale using reproject_interp. Visits are grouped into survey epochs (with automatic 120-day calendar windowing for continuous coverage near the North Ecliptic Pole).

4. Image-Measured Sub-Pixel Centroiding: Rather than drawing static catalog arrows, the pipeline measures true source centroids directly from the co-added SPHEREx pixels in each epoch using photutils.centroids (centroid_2dg, centroid_quadratic, centroid_com), displaying a fixed Epoch 1 crosshair alongside the measured inter-epoch shift in arcseconds.

5. Client-Side Float32 Rendering & On-the-Fly 102-Band Spectrophotometry: Decompressed Float32 science grids enable 60 FPS blinking, real-time dipole subtraction (Epoch B - Epoch A), two-epoch deep stacking (Epoch B + Epoch A), and False-Color IR RGB composites (R=D6, G=D4, B=D2). Clicking any pixel or source extracts background-subtracted circular aperture photometry (r = 2.5 px = 15.5"), evaluates the 2D tabular WCS-WAVE solution for exact wavelength and bandwidth (0.75–5.0 µm), propagates VARIANCE uncertainties, and builds SED-normalized multi-epoch light curves that eliminate artificial LVF filter-drift variability.

Validation on All 5 Official NASA Challenge Target

All five benchmark targets from the challenge brief are validated and pre-cached for instant (<10 ms) inspection:

- Barnard’s Star: High-proper-motion red dwarf (~10.4"/yr northward), revealing a crisp warm/cool dipole in difference mode and a ~2.5 px centroid shift across epochs.

- WISE 0855 (08h55m10.831s, -7d14m42.53s): Coldest known (250 K) Y4 sub-brown dwarf at 2.28 pc moving at 8.1"/yr westward; invisible in D1–D3 and Gaia DR3, but clearly detected and tracked in thermal channel D6 (4.42–5.00 µm).

- Epsilon Indi Ba/Bb: T1 + T6 binary brown dwarf pair separated from Epsilon Indi A, exhibiting deep H2O and CH4 absorption bands across D1–D4.

- RW Aurigae: Classical T Tauri variable star showing strong infrared circumstellar disk excess and multi-epoch variability.

- R Draconis: Mira AGB variable star near the North Ecliptic Pole with 2,494 overlapping visits partitioned into five clean epochs.

Intended Impact & Benefits

SPHEREx will image over a billion objects, far exceeding what any single research team can inspect manually. SPHEREx Blink turns a 30-minute Python FITS reduction workflow into a 1-second browser inspection, empowering citizen scientists (such as Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 volunteers), students, and astronomers to discover fast-moving brown dwarfs, Solar System objects, and infrared variables, and immediately verify their 0.75–5.0 µm molecular fingerprints (H2O, CO, CO2, CH4/PAH) in a single tool.

Tools, Languages & Architecture

- Backend: Python 3, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Astropy (io.fits, wcs, coordinates, stats), Astroquery (ipac.irsa), Reproject (reproject_interp), PhotUtils (aperture, centroids), NumPy, SciPy, Pillow.

- Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, HTML5 Canvas Float32 LUT renderer, custom SVG spectrophotometry charts, and shareable URL query state (?target=...&ra=...&dec=...&detector=...&mode=...&fov=...).

- AI/SI Transparency Attribution: LLM coding assistants (Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini) were used for React/TypeScript UI component scaffolding, CSS layout styling, English documentation/presentation editing, and API syntax lookup for astropy and photutils. All astronomical data comes strictly from real NASA/IPAC IRSA, ESA Gaia DR3, and CDS archives.
